title: Higher every week
note: Fictional unit. Values are illustrative; your system’s written baselines, action points, and the chief technician come first.
intro: You are the water technician. On Monday morning you read back over the log. The reverse osmosis product conductivity has risen each week for three weeks, from 12 to 18 µS/cm, and percent rejection has slipped from 98.4% to 97.5%. Both are still inside the unit’s action points.

choices.text: Report it today: within limits, but rising for three weeks.
choices.feedback: Most failures arrive slowly. Report direction, not only position. Falling rejection can mean membrane damage, scaling, or a leaking seal, and reporting now is the difference between a planned cleaning and a cancelled shift.

choices.text: Sign the log; everything is within limits.
choices.feedback: Within limits is position. A month of steady rise is direction, and direction is the warning.
choices.then: On reflection you report the trend that afternoon.

choices.text: Watch it for one more week, so you are sure it is a real trend before you raise it with anyone.
choices.feedback: Three weeks is already a trend. Report it now; watching continues.

vitals.weekend: Sat and Sun identical in every column

n2.scene: The relief technician’s Saturday and Sunday entries are identical in every column, to the decimal point.

choices.text: Report it as a gap; check the gauges; leave the entries as written.
choices.feedback: Identical readings day after day mean copied entries or a stuck gauge. Either way the record cannot show what the water was like. Never rewrite another person’s entries.

choices.text: Replace them with estimates based on Friday and Monday.
choices.feedback: Writing numbers nobody saw is falsifying the log. Report the gap; do not fill it.
choices.then: You leave the entries, report the gap, and check the gauges: one is stuck.

choices.text: It was a quiet weekend with no new patients, so the water probably did not change from one day to the next.
choices.feedback: Real readings vary a little every day. Identical numbers are a warning sign, not reassurance.
choices.then: You check the gauges: the product flow gauge is stuck. You report it.

vitals.culture: Rising 3 months running; still under limit

n3.scene: The monthly loop culture results have risen for three months in a row, still under the action level.
n3.prompt: What does it mean, and what do you do?

choices.text: Possible biofilm: report so disinfection is brought forward.
choices.feedback: Bacterial counts rising month to month but under the limit suggest biofilm. Disinfection may be due sooner than the schedule says. Waiting for the limit means waiting until the biofilm is established.
Passing is position; three months of rise is direction. Biofilm is far harder to remove once it is established.

choices.text: Resample next week to confirm the rise before reporting, since cultures can vary from month to month.
choices.feedback: A resample helps, but report the trend now so disinfection can be planned.

n4.scene: At 05:50 your morning round is complete and every reading today is within limits. The charge nurse passes the water room door: “Can we start?”
n4.prompt: What do you say and do?

choices.text: “Checks complete and within limits; released,” and sign.
choices.feedback: Release is the last step of the round. Say it in words and sign it. The nurse should never have to guess whether the water is ready.

choices.text: “Should be fine to start; I’ll finish the log in a minute and let you know if anything is off.”
choices.feedback: “Should be” is a guess. State that the checks are complete and within limits, and sign.

choices.text: Nod and go back to the log.
choices.feedback: A nod is not a release. Say it and sign it.

n5.prompt: What do you propose to the chief technician?

choices.text: Baselines and action points on the sheet, a signed weekly review, a monthly chart.
choices.feedback: The person who writes the same column every morning stops seeing a slow change. A second reader sees the whole week, and a chart shows the month. A number is easier to judge beside its reference.

choices.text: Remind the relief technician to be more careful.
choices.feedback: A reminder fixes one person for a week. Baselines on the sheet and a second reviewer fix the system.

choices.text: Buy a digital logger that records the readings automatically, so nothing depends on handwriting.
choices.feedback: It may help, but someone still has to read the record and act. Add baselines, action points, and a review routine.

end.title: Next month
end.text: The membrane was cleaned and its rejection recovered to 98.3%. The stuck gauge was replaced. Disinfection was brought forward and the next cultures fell. The log sheets now carry baselines and action points, and the weekly review is signed by the chief technician.

debrief:
What this case teaches

  • Report direction, not only position. “Within limits but rising” is a complete report.
  • Identical readings mean copying or a stuck gauge. Report the gap; never fill it.
  • Rising cultures under the limit suggest biofilm.
  • Release in words and in writing.
  • Baselines on the sheet and a second reviewer catch slow failures.
